title: Images that survive a slow connection
metaTitle: Images sized for a slow connection
excerpt: Send an image that matches the slot on the page. An oversized photograph delays the offer, and the alt text should still describe what is in the picture.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it. The desk with a code editor fits a piece about sizing images so a page still arrives.
caption: The picture should be only as heavy as the slot it fills. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How big should an image on a marketing page be?
faqs.answer: As wide as the slot it fills, at the pixel density of the screens you actually serve, and no wider. A 4000-pixel photograph in an 800-pixel column downloads detail nobody can see, so export a few widths and let the page choose. The hero can be larger than a thumbnail. It still does not need to be the original camera file.

faqs.question: Does alt text help the page load faster?
faqs.answer: No. Alt text is for people who do not see the image, and for the moment before the image arrives, so it should describe what is in the picture. It does not replace a properly sized file. A slow image with a stuffed alt attribute is still a slow image, and the description is worse.

faqs.question: What is a good loading target for the main image?
faqs.answer: web.dev's good threshold for Largest Contentful Paint is within 2.5 seconds of when the page starts loading, at the 75th percentile, split by mobile and desktop. If the hero photograph is the largest element, its file size and priority decide that moment. Reserve its space so the text does not jump when it lands.

markdown:
Send a picture that matches the hole it sits in. That is the practical core of responsive images performance. A 4000-pixel photograph in an 800-pixel column is a tax on the buyer. They pay in waiting, on the network they actually have, for pixels they cannot see. The alt text still describes the picture. It is not a place to hide the cost.

The hero is often the largest thing on the first screen. Until it appears, the page has not really arrived, even if the menu has. Treat the file as part of the sentence. A beautiful frame that shows up late is a late sentence.

## Match the slot, then the screen

Start from the layout, not from the camera. Measure the column. A content image in an article might be 800 pixels wide on a desktop layout and nearly the full width of a phone. A logo in the header might be 120 pixels wide. A product tile might be 400. Those are different files, or at least different widths of the same crop. One master exported at the largest size and dropped into every slot is how pages get heavy.

Account for dense screens without sending the master to everyone. A common pattern is to offer two or three widths and let the browser pick based on the slot and the device pixel ratio. A phone on a slow network should be allowed to take the smaller file. A wide desktop can take the sharper one. The markup has to tell the truth about how wide the image will be displayed. If you claim the image is full-bleed when it is a narrow column, the browser will pick a file that is too big.

Crop with the slot in mind. A wide landscape jammed into a square tile will be cut by the layout or letterboxed into a mess. Art-direct the crop for the phone if the subject sits at an edge. The point of a responsive image is not only fewer bytes. It is the right framing when the frame changes. A face sliced by a center crop on a phone is a content bug that happens to be implemented as CSS.

Keep the original in your working files. Publish the derivatives. The original is for the next crop, the next campaign, the print piece. It does not belong on the public page. Version the published file when the picture changes, so a cache that is doing its job does not show last season's product in this season's layout.

## The hero is a loading problem

web.dev's good line for Largest Contentful Paint is 2.5 seconds from the start of the load, judged at the 75th percentile of page loads, separately for mobile and desktop. On a marketing page the largest element is often the hero photograph or the headline. If it is the photograph, every extra hundred kilobytes is aimed directly at that clock.

Give the hero priority. It should not wait behind a gallery, a script, or a font. It should have its width and height set so the browser can reserve the box. Cumulative Layout Shift should stay at 0.1 or less. An image that arrives and shoves the headline down fails that test and feels like the page changed its mind.

Do not lazy-load the hero. Lazy loading is for images below the fold, where the download can wait until the person is near them. The first picture is the one they came to see. Marking it lazy is a way of making the largest content late on purpose.

Compression is a visual judgment, not only a slider. Look at the export at the display size, on a phone, not at 100 percent in an editor. A product edge, a face, and a block of type inside a photograph go soft before a texture does. If the picture contains words, prefer real HTML words beside it. Text baked into an image is blurry at the wrong size, invisible to a screen reader unless repeated, and frozen when the offer changes.

A store makes this concrete. On an ecommerce redesign such as Down the Cove, the product photograph is the thing the buyer is judging. It has to be sharp enough to trust and small enough to arrive. The rest of the page can be quiet. The product cannot be a blurry thumbnail stretched to hero size, and it cannot be a camera original either.

## Alt text describes the picture

Write the alt text from what is in the frame. "Founder at a bench, holding the finished ceramic cup" is alt text. "Best ceramic cups online buy now" is a slogan stuffed into an attribute. The alt text is read to people who do not see the image, and it is the description available before the file arrives. Both of those readers need the picture, not the campaign.

Decorative images can be empty in the alt attribute so assistive technology skips them. A divider, a texture, a background wash. If the image carries the meaning, it is not decorative. A hero that is the only explanation of the product needs a description. The caption can add the credit or the context. The alt text should still stand alone.

Do not repeat the caption and the alt text word for word if they sit next to each other and say the same sentence twice to a screen reader. Make the alt the visual description. Make the caption the extra fact, the credit, or the point in the argument. When there is no extra fact, a short alt and no caption is fine.

Keep alt text short enough to be spoken. A paragraph in the attribute is a speech the person did not ask to sit through. If the image needs a long description, put that description in the article, where everyone can read it, and keep the alt as a summary.

## Formats, motion, and what not to autoplay

Use a modern format for photographs, and keep a fallback your pipeline actually tests. The win is a smaller file at the same visual quality. The loss, if you are careless, is a pipeline that serves the modern file to browsers that handle it and a broken box to the rest. Test the fallback. A missing hero is worse than a heavier one.

Avoid video as a background for the sake of atmosphere. A looping clip in the hero is often the largest download on the page, it complicates reduced motion, and it pushes the real content aside. If motion explains a product change, a short clip with a poster image and a real control can earn its place. The poster should be a proper image with a reserved box, so the layout is stable before the video exists. Autoplay with sound is out. Autoplay without a still alternative is a problem for anyone who asked the system for less motion.

SVG is the right tool for logos, icons, and simple diagrams. It stays sharp at any size and it is usually small. It is the wrong tool for a photograph. Exporting a photo as a huge SVG, or as an uncompressed PNG because the export dialog was friendlier, is how a simple header becomes the slowest thing on the page. Match the format to the kind of picture.

Third-party embeds, a map, a social post, a review widget, bring their own images and their own scripts. They can dwarf the careful work you did on the hero. If you need them, place them lower, and do not let them decide the first paint. A screenshot you control is sometimes the better first view, with the live embed as a choice.

## Captions, crops, and the files you keep

A caption sits with the picture and says the extra fact: the place, the credit, the part of the product in the frame. It is not a second headline. Keep it in the text column, in the text face, shorter than the curiosity of the image. If you have nothing to add, skip the caption. A caption that repeats the alt text wastes the pause.

Keep source files out of the public bucket. The published object should be the cropped, compressed derivative, with a version in the name when the bytes change. Designers can keep masters in the project files. The site should request only what a slot can display. That split is what makes a later redesign possible without dragging four-thousand-pixel originals into every new template.

When a picture contains a face, a workspace, or a customer's environment, confirm you have permission to use it at the size the hero implies. A small reference photo becomes a different kind of exposure when it is the first screen. Technical performance does not answer that question. The review should, before the file is marked priority and sent to every visitor.

## A check on a slow phone

Throttle the network and reload the homepage. You are looking for three things. The headline is readable immediately. The hero arrives without jumping the text. The images further down do not all download before the visitor has scrolled. Then open an article and a product or project page and do it again. The homepage can be fast while the template you use fifty times is heavy.

Watch the width the browser actually requests. If you see the master file on a phone, the sizes in the markup are wrong. Fix the slot description. Do not only compress the master and hope. A compressed 4000-pixel file can still be far larger than a correctly sized 800-pixel file.

Look at the cache headers for images that rarely change. They should be safe to keep. When you replace a picture, change the URL or the version in the path so old caches do not win. A quiet image pipeline is part of the design system. It is not a chore for the night before launch.

Next.js can generate the widths and the markup from a source file so the page does not depend on someone remembering an export preset. That is worth using. It does not choose the crop, the priority, or the alt text. Those stay human. The founder should still be able to look at the phone and recognize the product before they feel the wait.

If the pictures on the site are working against the offer, [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) include the design and the build of pages where the image is sized for the slot it is in. Bring the heaviest template. The review is a slow load, not a zoomed-in mock.
